newsitem.title: CANADA: Report slams Canadian military over Somalia.
newsitem.headline: Report slams Canadian military over Somalia.

text.p: An independent commission on Wednesday issued a damning report on Canada's 1992-93 peacekeeping mission in Somalia, accusing the military of dishonoring its legacy, and blasting the government for trying to cover it up.

After two gruelling years of testimony, the Somalia Inquiry found that the torture and killing of Somali civilians during the mission reflected a lack of leadership, discipline and accountability in the Canadian military.

Impugning the reputation of officers right to the top of the military chain of command, the three-man commission welcomed the fact that many senior officers had left Canada's armed forces and suggested that others consider resigning.

"It is time for a new leadership to emerge in the Department of National Defense and the Canadian Forces and it is time for that new leadership to carry the forces in a new direction," Commission Chairman Gilles Letourneau told a news conference.
His two colleagues, Robert Rutherford and Peter Desbarats, were more specific, declaring that acting chief of defense staff Vice Admiral Larry Murray should not remain the head of Canada's military.
"I'm of the opinion that he's not the best man for the job," said Rutherford.

On March 4, 1993, Canadian soldiers worried about looters shot two unarmed Somalis in the back as they fled, killing one of them. Twelve days later they tortured to death a 16-year-old Somali boy named Shidane Arone.
The commission found excessive force was used in the shooting incident and that it was immediately covered up by Defense Headquarters in Ottawa.

Warning flags should have been heeded and discipline imposed before the incidents, the commission said. Members of the elite Canadian Airborne Regiment, the unit that served in Somalia, had set off ammunition and pyrotechnics illegally and set a car afire before they were deployed.
Subsequently published videos showed racist hazing practices that forced the Airborne Regiment to be disbanded.

The commission said many Canadian peacekeepers deserved a medal for their service in Somalia, but the force as a whole was "ill-prepared and rudderless...(and) fell inevitably into the mire that became the Somali debacle.
"As a result, a proud legacy was dishonored," the commissioners said.
The incidents and their immediate aftermath, which are known in Canada as the "Somalia Affair", occurred during a Conservative government, which was defeated in a 1993 election.

The commission, which was appointed by the Liberal Party government of Prime Minister Jean Chretien and empowered only to investigate and make recommendations to the government, slammed its creators, charging the administration with "deep and moral legal failings."
The panel implicated Chretien's government in delaying its access to key military documents, while others were altered or not handed over at all and witnesses lied or fudged testimony.
"The testimony of many witnesses was characterized by inconsistency, improbability, implausibility, evasiveness, selective recollection, half-truths, and plain lies.
"Indeed, on some issues we encountered what can only be described as a wall of silence...evidently a strategy of calculated deception," the commission said.
It assailed the government for cutting short the inquiry just as it was getting to many senior leaders.

"The government abandoned its earlier declared interest in holding to account senior leaders and officials who participated in the planning and execution of the mission and responded to the problems that arose," it said.
Former Liberal Defense Minister Doug Young, defeated in Canada's federal election last month, ordered in January that the commission must wind up its work by the end of June.
Current Defense Minister Art Eggleton criticized the overall tone of the commission's findings and said it was time to stop pointing fingers and get on with reforms.
"The commission report paints an excessively negative picture of the Canadian Forces that is inconsistent with the positive record of achievement both at home and abroad."
